angle: Sequence models pay off with long, ordered sessions and a fast-churning catalog - otherwise you buy latency for nothing.

title: Projecting BrowseComp-Plus onto ClimbMix: Toward More Realistic Corpora for Agentic Search
summary: The BrowseComp-Plus benchmark disentangled the evaluation of agentic search by replacing opaque web search with a fixed corpus, so that an agent's role can be separated from the retriever's. That corpus, however, holds only about 100K documents and was assembled from the supporting documents of the benchmark's own queries plus mined hard negatives, so the evidence and the distractors were both selected per query. We introduce $\text{BrowseComp-Plus}_{\text{CM}}$, which keeps the BrowseComp-Plus questions but relocates their evidence to ClimbMix, a 400B-token, 553M-document mixture of web text released by NVIDIA for pre-training language models and built without reference to any benchmark. Ou
angle: A benchmark can look realistic while still encoding its own relevance judgments: moving the same questions to an independently collected corpus is a useful test of whether an agent retrieves evidence or merely exploits query-specific document construction.
why_now: A newly proposed corpus directly addresses whether agentic-search gains survive outside benchmark-curated evidence and negatives.

title: SCoRD: Semantic-Assisted Continual Retriever-Reranker Distillation for LLM-Based Recommendation
summary: Recommendation systems increasingly adopt a two-stage pipeline, where an ID-based retriever retrieves candidates and an LLM-based reranker refines their rankings. To improve retrieval quality, reranker-to-retriever distillation is commonly used to transfer the reranker's knowledge to the retriever. For practical deployment, however, this pipeline must continually adapt to evolving interests and incoming interactions. A naive solution is to repeatedly update the LLM reranker and distill its latest knowledge, but this incurs prohibitive costs. Updating the retriever alone is cheaper, but its limited capacity makes adaptation from sparse data difficult. We propose SCoRD, a continual knowledge d
angle: Continual retriever distillation should be treated as a teacher-refresh problem, not simply a retriever-training problem: the practical win comes from adapting a cheap student without repeatedly paying for an evolving LLM reranker.
why_now: Continual adaptation and the cost of LLM-based ranking are immediate production concerns as recommendation stacks add LLM rerankers.

title: Do Sequential Recommendation Benchmarks Really Require Higher-Order Sequence Modelling?
summary: Sequential recommenders increasingly use language-model architectures designed to capture complex, context-dependent interactions. Yet it remains unclear whether widely used benchmarks actually require this modelling capacity. We investigate this question using two simple, recency-weighted pairwise probes that do not learn higher-order sequence representations: Sequential Rules (SeqRules) and our Probabilistic Collaborative Transition Model (PCTM). Using the evaluation protocol of eSASRec, at least one probe exceeds our eSASRec reproduction by 15-38% on three Amazon datasets and by 4.4% on MovieLens-1M, but trails it by 27.3% on MovieLens-20M. On the four remaining datasets, at least one pro
angle: Before investing in higher-order sequence models, run a recency-weighted transition baseline: if it beats the neural model by 15–38%, the benchmark may be measuring short-term item transitions rather than genuine sequence understanding.
why_now: The paper challenges current sequential-recommendation architecture assumptions with unusually large baseline gains on widely used datasets.

title: Training-Free LLM-Based Recommendation with Post-LLM Item Refinement Using Collaborative Signals
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for training-free recommendation, but LLM-generated user interests are often too broad for fine-grained item retrieval. Existing methods incorporate collaborative filtering (CF) signals in a pre-LLM manner through candidate reranking or prompt augmentation, yielding limited gains. We propose CoRRe, a training-free recommendation framework with a post-LLM paradigm that injects CF signals into LLM-generated item representations, which are later matched with LLM-generated user interests for ranking. Specifically, CoRRe refines the directions of item embeddings using an item-item co-purchase graph and their magnitudes using item popularity. Experim
angle: When an LLM understands user intent but cannot distinguish nearby items, collaborative signals may belong after semantic generation—not in the prompt—because graph structure and popularity correct different errors in the item representation.
why_now: This is a timely counterpoint to training-free LLM recommendation approaches that treat broad semantic matching as sufficient for fine-grained ranking.

title: SSR-GRPO: Integrating Supervision and Semantic IDs into Reinforcement Learning for Dense Retrieval in E-commerce
summary: Embedding-based retrieval (EBR) is pivotal in e-commerce search but often struggles with complex semantics. While recent methods often fine-tune large language models (LLMs) for representation learning, they typically lack robust mechanisms for handling complex and implicit semantics. While Retrieval-GRPO (R-GRPO) recently introduced reinforcement learning to dense retrieval, it suffers from noisy top-K candidates due to limited batch sampling and biased relevance assessments caused by using similarly trained LLMs as reward models. To tackle these issues, we propose Supervised Retrieval-GRPO with Semantic Identifiers (SSR-GRPO). Specifically, our method first proposes a dual-perspective fram
angle: RL for dense retrieval is only as credible as its candidate sampling and reward construction; adding supervision and semantic IDs may matter less than removing the self-referential bias in LLM-generated relevance rewards.
why_now: Dense-retrieval systems are increasingly experimenting with RL, making reward noise and biased top-K sampling practical deployment concerns.

title: Quantization Beyond Uniform Bit Allocation
summary: Quantization is a fundamental technique to handle the growing sizes of embeddings generated by modern models. Existing quantization schemes are largely embedding agnostic and allocate bits uniformly across dimensions. However, recent models produce embeddings with significant geometric structure. In this work, we investigate whether a variable bit allocation scheme can improve quantization quality under a fixed memory budget. We propose a simple variable bit allocation framework that partitions an embedding into contiguous buckets and allocates storage non-uniformly across them. Using a greedy allocation strategy, we instantiate this framework for both Product Quantization (PQ) and Scalar Qu
angle: Embedding compression should spend bits where the representation carries usable geometry, not assume every dimension deserves equal precision—but the practical test is whether the allocation survives index updates and distribution drift, not just reconstruction error.
why_now: Embedding memory costs keep rising, making a concrete alternative to uniform quantization immediately relevant to retrieval teams.

title: rEDMRec: Distilling Large Language Model Reasoning into an Editable Experience Memory for Recommendation
summary: Large language models can improve recommendation quality by reasoning explicitly over user history and candidate items - for example, extracting a user's preferences or explaining why one item fits better than another - rather than mapping history directly to a ranked list. This reasoning, however, is expensive to repeat on every ranking request and, once produced, is typically consumed once and discarded, leaving it neither reusable across future requests nor easy to inspect or correct as user tastes drift. Our insight is that reasoning does not need to be regenerated at every call if it can instead be compressed once into a compact, structured memory that a lightweight model retrieves from
angle: The valuable architectural move is turning expensive LLM reasoning into editable, reusable user state; the production question is whether stale or confidently wrong memories are easier to detect than repeatedly generated reasoning.
why_now: LLM-enhanced recommendation is moving from demos toward serving constraints, making reusable reasoning state a concrete systems trade-off.

title: Think-to-Personalize: Unifying Reasoning and Retrieval for User-Centric Personalized Dense Retrieval
summary: Dense retrieval has become a cornerstone of modern local-lifestyle e-commerce search by encoding queries and items into semantic embedding spaces. While recent advancements have transitioned from BERT-based embedding models to Large Language Models (LLMs), most approaches still treat LLMs as static text encoders, neglecting their inherent reasoning capabilities. Furthermore, standard dense retrieval models remain query-centric, which is insufficient in e-commerce scenarios where sparse and ambiguous queries create an intent gap that can only be bridged by the rich context of user history. Meanwhile, existing personalized retrieval methods typically rely on implicit embedding interactions, wh
angle: Personalized retrieval should use history to resolve ambiguous intent before asking a dense encoder to represent the query, but reasoning-heavy retrieval must prove its latency and candidate-recall gains against a simpler user-conditioned encoder.
why_now: Search teams are actively deciding whether LLM reasoning belongs in candidate generation or only in later ranking.

In Part 3, we will explore how we designed a fast, flexible serving layer to efficiently query the graph. Introduction In Part 1 of this series, we described w
angle: Netflix’s graph serving layer is interesting not because it uses gRPC, but because its query API turns a billion-edge storage problem into an explicit latency-and-flexibility tradeoff that a smaller team should solve with narrower query contracts instead.

title: GenRec: Towards LLM-Native Recommendation at Netflix
summary: Authors: Ying Li , Arjun Rao , Shradha Sehgal Introduction Recommendations sit at the heart of the Netflix experience. Our current production models rely on thousands of hand‑crafted features over users, items, and interactions, along with specialized architectures for sequence modeling, feature interactions, and multi‑task objectives. This stack has evolved over many years to support diverse content types (movies, series, games, live, podcasts) and product surfaces, but its complexity makes it costly to onboard new use cases: adding a content type or surface can require significant feature engineering, architecture change, infrastructure work, and experimentation. At the same time, large la
angle: Netflix’s LLM-native recommendation direction attacks the hidden cost of recommender systems—adding a new content type or surface—not necessarily ranking quality, while moving complexity into representation, evaluation, and serving constraints.

title: GenPage: Towards End-to-End Generative Homepage Construction at Netflix
summary: Authors: Lequn Wang , J iangwei Pan , and Linas Baltrunas Figure 1. Autoregressive homepage generation. Almost every part of it is personalized, including which rows appear, which entities show up within those rows, and how everything is arranged on the page. Constructing that homepage is a genuinely hard problem. It is not simply producing one ranked list. The homepage is a structured, two-dimensional layout, made up of
angle: Generating a homepage autoregressively treats layout diversity and row interactions as part of recommendation, but a smaller team should copy the structured decision framing rather than the full generative surface because exposure constraints and debugging become much harder.

summary: TL;DR: We introduce Stochastic Primal-Dual Decoding (SPDD), a lightweight inference-time method that steers... The post Balancing Multiple Objectives in Generative Recommendations with Adaptive Decoding appeared first on Spotify Engineering .
angle: Adaptive decoding is a compelling way to enforce multiple recommendation objectives without retraining the model, but its production value depends on whether the objective weights remain calibrated under changing candidate distributions and whether the extra decoding cost fits the latency budget.

summary: Podcasts are one of Spotify’s fastest-growing content verticals, with over 750 million users discovering... The post Cold-Starting Podcast Ads with Multi-Task Learning appeared first on Spotify Engineering .
angle: The useful lesson from Spotify’s podcast-ad cold start is that multi-task learning can transfer mature user and ad signals into a sparse vertical, but only if task relatedness is measured rather than assumed—otherwise the shared representation transfers bias too.

summary: Spotify’s mission is to connect every listener with the right audio and help every creator be discovered... The post Teaching Large Language Models to Speak Spotify: How Semantic IDs Enable Personalization appeared first on Spotify Engineering .
angle: Semantic IDs make generative recommendation look like language modeling, but they relocate the hard recommender problem into the token vocabulary: ID stability, collisions, granularity, and updates matter more than the LLM analogy.

summary: Part 1 of 2 Authors Personalization (Homefeed): Yuke Yan, Chuxi Wang, Andreanne Lemay, Olafur Gudmundsson, Anna Kiyantseva, Krystal Benitez, Jongho Kim, Jiacong He, Rahul Goutam, James Li, Dylan Wang User Understanding: Simin Li, Sufyan Suliman, Yingjian Ding, Hongbo Deng Data Science: Armando Ordorica, Yan Chen, Ellie Zhang, Karim Wahba Introduction Pinterest’s mission is to help people discover the inspiration to create a life they love. Our recommendation system serves hundreds of millions of users, surfacing billions of Pins across interests ranging from home renovation to meal planning to wedding decor. The home feed , where much of that discovery happens, is powered by a multi-stage pi
angle: Pinterest’s use-case representation suggests that improving the system’s model of why a user is browsing can outperform adding another generic user embedding, but the transferable lesson is to represent intent at the interaction level rather than copy Pinterest’s architecture.

Multi-node distributed training is the key to unlocking the next level of that capacity. ¹ But when we first attempted
angle: Pinterest’s distributed training story is worth reading less as a scaling victory and more as a reminder that near-linear throughput depends on removing communication and input-pipeline bottlenecks, not simply adding GPUs; a 10-engineer team should copy the profiling discipline, not the cluster design.

title: Making User-Sequence Data More Cost-Efficient, Faster, and Easier to Use
summary: Authors ( listed alphabetically ) Ads Feature Engineering Infra team: Ajay Venkatakrishnan, Le Zhang Core ML Infra team: Eric Shang, Pihui Wei ML Data team: Connor Votroubek, Yi He User Understanding team: Camilo Munoz, Simin Li If you work on ranking, retrieval, or recommendation systems, you’ve probably asked for some version of the same thing: “Give me the last N meaningful actions this user took, with the right enrichments, in a format that’s easy to train and serve ML models.” On paper, that sounds simple. In practice, “user sequences” often become one of the most expensive and fragile parts of the ML data stack. They end up powering everything from training datasets to offline analysis
angle: The overlooked recommender-system bottleneck is often not the sequence model but repeatedly reconstructing user histories across training, analysis, and serving; the transferable lesson is to treat user sequences as a governed data product with one canonical representation.

title: Enhancing Ad Relevance: Integrating Real-Time Context into Sequential Recommender Models
summary: Huiqin Xin | Machine Learning Engineer II, Ads Vertical Modeling; Lakshmi Manoharan | Senior Machine Learning Engineer, Ads Vertical Modeling; Karthik Jayasurya | Staff Machine Learning Engineer, Ads Signals; Ziwei Guo | Senior Machine Learning Engineer, Ads Vertical Modeling; Alina Liviniuk | Machine Learning Engineer II, Ads Vertical Modeling Motivation: The Need for Real-Time Context In a previous post , Ads Candidate Generation using Behavioral Sequence Modeling , we introduced a candidate generator (CG) that uses a Transformer-based two-tower model to leverage a user’s offsite conversion history — a powerful signal — to predict future interactions with advertisers and specific products.
angle: Adding real-time context to a sequential recommender is not merely a feature win: it exposes the mismatch between slowly changing behavioral history and rapidly changing purchase intent, so the production design should explicitly separate those timescales.

In order to know if a given Pin is relevan
angle: Feature trimming at the serving boundary reframes network optimization as model design: eliminating low-value payloads can improve latency and cost without retraining the ranker, but only if the team measures feature-value loss rather than optimizing bytes blindly.

title: From Clicks to Conversions: Architecting Shopping Conversion Candidate Generation at Pinterest
summary: Authors: Richard Huang | Machine Learning Engineer II; Yu Liu | Senior Machine Learning Engineer; Ziwei Guo | Senior Machine Learning Engineer; Andy Mao | Staff Machine Learning Engineer; Supeng Ge | Sr. Staff Machine Learning Engineer Introduction At Pinterest, conversion ads are crucial for matching users with products they are likely to purchase, boosting value for both users and advertisers¹. While conversion actions like checkout or add-to-cart are highly valuable, they are also technically challenging to optimize for. Because they occur offsite, conversion events are significantly sparser and noisier than onsite engagement signals. Historically, Pinterest’s shopping ads retrieval relie
angle: Conversion retrieval is fundamentally a sparse-label and delayed-feedback problem, so the important design choice is how to trade recall for signal reliability before ranking—not simply how to build a stronger embedding model.

title: Personalizing Airbnb search by learning from the guest journey
summary: How we built a Transformer-based sequence model that encodes years of guest behavior to surface the right listings at the right time. By: Daochen Zha , Chun How Tan , Xin Liu , Bin Xu , Han Zhao , Xiaowei Liu , Jun Shi , Tracy Yu , Hui Gao , Huiji Gao , Liwei He , Michael Kinoti , Stephanie Moyerman , and Sanjeev Katariya Introduction Planning a trip on Airbnb rarely happens in a single session. A guest searching for a place to stay in San Francisco might browse dozens of listings over several days, leaving behind a trail of views. Typically, over a period of years, that same guest will have accumulated many previous bookings, reviews, and the occasional cancellation. Taken together, these e
angle: Airbnb’s guest-journey model illustrates why sequence length alone is not personalization: years of behavior must be filtered through trip-stage and current intent, otherwise historical bookings can overwhelm the signal for the trip being planned.

title: From User Sequences to Scaling Laws: A Multi-Stage Architecture for Meta’s Ads Ranking
summary: Every day, Meta’s recommendation platforms handle billions of user interactions, generating rich temporal signals that capture individual preferences and intent across products, ads, and content. angle: Meta’s multi-stage sequence architecture suggests that scaling laws are most useful when applied unevenly: spend model capacity on the stages with enough candidate volume and training signal, rather than making every ranker equally large.

angle: The compelling lesson from GEM is that recommender foundation-model economics are governed by end-to-end MFU and pipeline efficiency, not headline parameter count; a smaller model with fewer stalls can beat a larger one in useful training progress per dollar.

title: Exploring Hierarchical Interest Representation For Meta Ads Deep Funnel Optimization
summary: Hierarchical Interest Representation is a research area for Meta Ads. We’re exploring an upstream representation layer over the universe of Ads entities – users, advertisers, products, services – learning unified embeddings that connect users’ inferred interests with the breadth of what advertisers offer in their deep funnel ads. The innovations in Hierarchical Interest Representation are [...] Read More... The post Exploring Hierarchical Interest Representation For Meta Ads Deep Funnel Optimization appeared first on Engineering at Meta .
angle: Hierarchical interest representations are attractive for deep-funnel ads because they can connect users and commercial entities across abstraction levels, but the production question is whether the hierarchy improves sparse conversion supervision or merely makes embeddings harder to debug.

title: Modernizing the Meta Ads Service With an Open-Source Kernel Scheduler
summary: TL; DR At Meta’s scale, a few milliseconds of latency degradation can have a significant negative impact on ads performance. When a Linux kernel upgrade risked regressing latency across Meta’s ad serving fleet, we turned to sched_ext — the upstream, BPF-based extensible scheduling framework — to build a scheduling policy customized to the Ads delivery [...] Read More... angle: Meta’s scheduler work shows that at ads-serving scale, a kernel-level latency regression can matter more than an application optimization—but a 10-person team should first isolate critical workloads and measure tail latency before adopting custom scheduling.
why_now: A fresh Meta engineering writeup provides a concrete case study for discussing the often-overlooked systems layer beneath ranking and serving.

title: Training an LLM-RecSys Hybrid for Steerable Recs with Semantic IDs
summary: An LLM that can converse in English & item IDs, and make recommendations w/o retrieval or tools.
angle: Semantic IDs can make an LLM produce recommendations directly, but the production trade is moving complexity from retrieval into catalog representation, item churn handling, and reliable next-token generation.
why_now: LLM-recommender hybrids are attracting attention, while this framing gives practitioners a reason to question whether removing retrieval actually removes system complexity.

title: Improving Recommendation Systems & Search in the Age of LLMs
summary: Model architectures, data generation, training paradigms, and unified frameworks inspired by LLMs.
angle: LLM-inspired recommenders will not materially improve a system whose bottleneck is feedback-biased data and a misaligned objective; the useful transfer is in data generation and training workflows, not automatically replacing retrieval and ranking models.
why_now: LLM-style architectures and unified recommendation/search systems are attracting attention, making it timely to separate transferable training ideas from architecture cargo culting.

One of them is definitely "how to make things look good, even when they aren't." I'm guilty too, but trying to get better every day. 1. For single-hop retrieval, make sure there are no distractors and context is useless The three most cooperative settings for compression / sparsity are: Needle in a haystack with a single OOD key-value pair and context built out of a repeated sente
angle: Many sparse-attention and KV-compression wins are benchmark-design wins: remove distractors, use friendly retrieval patterns, and measure average accuracy instead of the failure cases that production traffic actually contains.
why_now: Efficient inference claims are increasingly important as long-context workloads compete for memory and latency budgets, so benchmark validity is worth scrutinizing now.

title: The spectral neuron - an ML primitive for scalable and interpretable models [R]
summary: Worked some time ago on one of the ad teams at Yahoo, and this grew out of a question I kept returning to while there are there "simple" models that are both simple, scalable, interpretable, and controllable at the same time? Decided to explore it, first in a blog (starting here ), then in a new preprint "The Spectral Neuron", built by distilling latest blog-posts into a manuscript, I study models of the form: 𝑓(𝒙) = 𝛌ₖ(𝐀₀ + 𝚺ᵢ 𝑥ᵢ𝐀ᵢ). Manuscript : https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08003 Code : https://github.com/alexshtf/spectral_neuron_paper Looks like a simple on-liner, but many interesting aspects hide there. How expressive does the model become as the matrices grow? What can
angle: The spectral neuron is interesting less because its one-line matrix form is novel than because it may offer controllability and interpretability for tabular or ranking models—but those benefits only matter if it beats strong tree and linear baselines at comparable parameter and serving costs.
why_now: The preprint is new and offers a timely opportunity to examine whether a compact, interpretable primitive can address practical model-governance and scaling constraints rather than merely add another expressive architecture.
